Title: Do Protective Perturbations Really Protect Portrait Privacy under Real-world Image Transformations?
Text:
Do Protective Perturbations Really Protect Portrait Privacy under
Real-world Image Transformations?

Wu Zhijing

Abstract
Proactive defense methods protect portrait images from unautho-
rized editing or talking face generation (TFG) by introducing pixel-
level protective perturbations, and have already attracted increasing
attention for privacy protection. In real-world scenarios, images
inevitably undergo various transformations during cross-device
display and dissemination—such as scale transformations and color
compression—that directly alter pixel values. However, it remains
unclear whether such pixel-level modifications affect the effec-
tiveness of existing proactive defense methods that rely on pixel-
level perturbations. To solve this problem, we conduct a systematic
evaluation of representative proactive defenses under image trans-
formation. The evaluated methods are selected to span different
generation architectures such as diffusion and GAN-based models,
as well as defense scopes covering both portrait and natural images,
and are assessed using both qualitative and quantitative metrics for
subjective and objective comparison. Experimental results indicate
that defense methods based on pixel-level perturbations struggle
to withstand common image transformations, posing a risk of de-
fense failure in real-world applications. To further highlight this
risk, we propose a simple yet effective purification framework by
leveraging the vulnerabilities induced by real-world image trans-
formations. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed
method can efficiently remove protective perturbations with low
computational cost, highlighting previously overlooked risks to the
research community. Our code is available at xxx.
Keywords
Portrait Privacy Protection; Adversarial Purification; Super-Resolution

1
Introduction
The rapid advancement of generative adversarial networks (GANs)
and diffusion models has substantially accelerated the development
of AI-generated content (AIGC) technologies, such as image edit-
ing and talking face generation (TFG) [2, 6, 7, 37]. While these
advances demonstrate remarkable technical capabilities, they also
substantially increase the risk of malicious misuse, including fraud,
political manipulation, and the dissemination of misinformation.
To mitigate these risks, a variety of defense techniques have been
proposed and can be broadly categorized into passive detection and
proactive defense [9]. Passive detection methods attempt to iden-
tify whether facial content has been edited or forged by training
generative content detectors [45]. In contrast, proactive defense
methods proactively interfere with the generation process by in-
jecting imperceptible protective perturbations into images, causing
the synthesized outputs to degrade [10, 26, 30]. By preventing pri-
vacy abuse at the source, proactive defense has therefore attracted
increasing attention. Recent studies demonstrate that such pertur-
bations can effectively prevent generative models from modifying
facial attributes or identity [13, 30], or from synthesizing talking
portrait videos using TFG models [10, 28] in local test.

Compared to local testing, images may inevitably undergo vari-
ous image transformations during real-world transmission. Recent
studies have investigated how image compression during dissemi-
nation on online social network platforms affects the effectiveness
of proactive defenses [26, 43]. However, they largely overlook ef-
fects of other transformations. For example, to accommodate het-
erogeneous display devices with varying resolutions and screen
sizes, images are frequently resized via interpolation-based resam-
pling operations. Since most existing defense algorithms are not
explicitly designed to handle such transformations and are highly
sensitive to scale variations, even benign user behaviors—such as
taking screenshots for sharing or archiving—can unintentionally
degrade their protective effectiveness, as illustrated in Fig. 1. Similar
vulnerabilities also arise from color compression during mobile pho-
tography, platform-specific image processing, and storage formats,
all of which introduce irreversible modifications to pixel statistics.
As a consequence, if defense methods fail to adapt to these diverse
and often inevitable real-world transformations, they may substan-
tially overestimate their robustness, ultimately providing users with
a false sense of security.
In this work, we systematically examine the practical viability of
protection methods based on adversarial perturbations under realis-
tic deployment conditions. Our study focuses on two representative
application scenarios: (i) protecting facial attributes from malicious
manipulation, and (ii) preventing portrait images from being ex-
ploited for TFG. In terms of evaluation coverage, we consider a
broad range of open-source defense models targeting both GAN-
based and diffusion-based AIGC frameworks, encompassing general
defenses as well as specific, open-source methods. Moreover, our
evaluation spans both widely cited representative approaches and
recently released state-of-the-art models. Extensive experiments
demonstrate that under common real-world transformations—such
as resolution changes and color compression—protective perturba-
tions often fail to reliably prevent portrait editing or talking-face
synthesis.
To further raise awareness of these risks within the community,
we propose a simple yet effective training-free purification method,
termed Transformation-Induced Purification via Region-wise Super-
Resolution (TIP-RSR), by exploiting the above vulnerabilities. The
proposed approach adopts differentiated purification strategies for
facial regions and background areas in portrait images. Experimen-
tal results show that TIP-RSR can efficiently remove protective
perturbations while maximally preserving the structural integrity
and visual fidelity of the original image. These findings underscore
the urgent need to revisit the robustness assumptions of existing
protection methods and to explore more resilient solutions for mit-
igating privacy abuse risks posed by modern AIGC technologies
Our contributions are summarized as follows:
• We conduct a systematic evaluation of state-of-the-art and
prevalent proactive defense methods under two representa-
tive real-world image transformations: scale variations and
color compression.
• We demonstrate that common real-world transformations
can significantly degrade the effectiveness of protective per-
turbations, causing existing methods to fail to reliably pre-
vent portrait editing and TFG in practice.
• We introduce TIP-RSR, a training-free purification approach
that effectively removes protective perturbations from pro-
tective images while preserving most of the original struc-
tural information, exposing previously overlooked vulnera-
bilities in current protection methods.
2
Related Works
2.1
Talking Face Generation
Generating realistic talking portrait videos conditioned on a given
audio signal and a target portrait image is a core task in TFG,
and has attracted considerable attention due to its broad practi-
cal applications. Early works primarily focused on synthesizing
lip movements that are highly synchronized with the input audio,
achieving notable success in scenarios such as video translation
and dubbing [16, 25]. More recently, the development of diffusion
models has substantially advanced the TFG field [12, 21]. The Hallo
[37] series introduces hierarchical audio-driven visual synthesis
modules along with data augmentation strategies, enabling high-
resolution, pose-controllable, and long-duration talking portrait
video generation. Loopy [14] exploits long-term motion dependen-
cies to synthesize vivid talking portrait videos with subtle facial
details, without relying on explicit motion constraints or prede-
fined templates. Ditto [17] further improves diffusion-based TFG
frameworks by enabling streaming processing, real-time inference,
and low first-frame latency.
2.2
Image Editing
In the field of AIGC, image editing has been widely recognized
as a task of significant practical importance. Early studies were
predominantly built upon GAN-based frameworks, enabling the
manipulation of specific visual attributes such as hair color, skin
tone, and even facial identity [6, 7]. More recently, the rapid devel-
opment of multimodal large-scale models has made it possible to
directly edit images according to natural language instructions. For
example, InstructPix2Pix [2] leverages multiple large models to con-
struct bimodal paired data, enabling instruction-following image
editing guided by human-written instructions. HiDream-E1-1 [3]
adopts a sparse Diffusion Transformer architecture together with a
dynamic mixture-of-experts design, achieving a favorable trade-off
between computational efficiency and image generation quality.
Qwen-Image [36] further improves visual consistency and seman-
tic coherence between edited images and their originals through
comprehensive data engineering, progressive learning strategies,
enhanced multi-task training paradigms, and scalable infrastructure
optimizations. While these advances in image editing and TFG sub-
stantially improve controllability, fidelity, and usability, they also
exacerbate ethical and societal risks, particularly raising concerns
about privacy violations and the misuse of AIGC.
2.3
Proactive Defense
To protect personal images from potential misuse by TFG and image
editing models, several recent studies have explored perturbation-
based protection by injecting imperceptible noise to disrupt the
generation process. FaceLock [30] integrates a facial recognition
model as an adversary into the diffusion loop, inducing substan-
tial visual discrepancies between edited outputs and the original

images. DF-RAP [26] explicitly incorporates compression opera-
tions commonly used on online social network platforms, thereby
improving the robustness of image editing defenses under practi-
cal deployment conditions. The Silencer [10] series aims to silence
speech generation by applying protective perturbations to the input
images, achieving effective defense against TFG methods. Despite
their effectiveness, these approaches generally overlook the fact
that images may undergo multiple resolution changes and color
compression operations during real-world dissemination, which
can significantly undermine the reliability of such protections in
practice.
3
Evaluation of the Protective Perturbation
3.1
Dataset and Selected Models
Our evaluation focuses on two key application scenarios: facial
attribute editing and TFG. To ensure that the evaluation metrics
more accurately reflect the effectiveness of defense methods, we
adopt the CelebA-HQ [15] dataset, as it is explicitly used in the
original papers of the evaluated methods, thereby minimizing po-
tential interference introduced by out-of-domain data. Considering
the substantial computational cost of large-scale evaluation, follow-
ing the work of Ditto [17], we select a subset of the CelebA-HQ
dataset consisting of the first 100 facial images. For GAN-based
facial attribute editing experiments, we employ DF-RAP [26] and
AntiForgery [31] as representative proactive defense methods to
protect portrait images against StarGAN-based attacks [7]. No-
tably, DF-RAP explicitly accounts for the influence of online social
network platforms, making it particularly suitable for evaluating
defense robustness under realistic dissemination conditions. For
diffusion-based model experiments, we adopt two recently released
open-source defense methods, FaceLock [30] and FaceShield [13],
to protect portrait images against attacks generated using Instruct-
Pix2Pix [2] and IP-Adapter [39]. For talking-face generation (TFG)
attacks, we evaluate a set of general-purpose defense methods, in-
cluding AdvDM(-) [38], MIST [19], and PhotoGuard [27], together
with the task-specific defense Silencer-I [10]. All methods are ap-
plied to protect portrait images against attacks generated by Hallo
[37].
3.2
Evaluation Metrics
To investigate how common image processing operations affect
protective perturbations, we apply three representative transforma-
tions to adversarially protected samples: JPEG compression with
a quality factor of 75, image resizing, and a combination of JPEG
compression followed by resizing. The transformed images are then
used as inputs for both image editing and TFG tasks. Followed by
DF-RAP [26], qualitative and quantitative analyses are conducted
by comparing the generated results with those obtained using un-
defended clean images as inputs.
For image editing attacks, we measure the PSNR and SSIM to
quantify the distortion between images generated before and af-
ter defense. In addition, FID [11], LPIPS [42], and BRISQUE [22]
are used to assess the visual quality of adversarial examples and
generated images. The same set of metrics is also used to evaluate
the overall quality of adversarial examples. For TFG attacks, PSNR
and SSIM are adopted to evaluate the visual quality of generated
videos, while Sync-C [8] and M-LMD [5] are employed to assess
audio–visual synchronization.
3.3
Experimental Results
The experimental results indicate that existing defense methods
struggle to remain effective under common image transformations.
As shown in Table 1 and Table 2, when protected images processed
by JPEG compression and resizing are used for image editing and
TFG, the resulting outputs become noticeably closer to those gen-
erated from clean images, compared to results obtained from un-
transformed protected inputs. For image editing tasks, this trend
is reflected by clear improvements in PSNR and SSIM, along with
consistent reductions in FID, LPIPS, and BRISQUE. For TFG, in
addition to improved visual fidelity, the generated results exhibit
lip-motion patterns that are more similar to those produced from
clean inputs, as evidenced by increased Sync-C scores and M-LMD.
Additional quantitative results for settings involving resize-only
and JPEG-only transformations are provided in the Table 9 and
Table 8 (Appendix).
Qualitative results show that existing defense models tend to
lose their effectiveness after undergoing scale variations, and this
degradation becomes more pronounced when scale changes are
combined with JPEG compression, as illustrated in Fig. 2 and Fig
3. The evaluation results further suggest that common real-world
image processing operations should be explicitly considered during
model design, which otherwise may result in overestimated defense
performance and a false sense of security for users. For instance,
DF-RAP exhibits relatively stronger robustness against JPEG com-
pression, as it explicitly accounts for compression operations, which
is commonly applied by online social network platforms, during its
design. Such targeted modeling strategies remain inherently fragile.
For instance, they struggle to defend against joint attacks under
the C&R setting, where compression and resizing are applied in
combination. This observation suggests that explicitly modeling
a single image transformation in isolation may not constitute a
robust solution. Moreover, during the C&R process, the semantic
content of images is largely preserved, while subtle protective per-
turbations are effectively removed. This behavior can be attributed
to the fact that image transformations in real-world dissemination
pipelines are typically designed to be perceptually inconspicuous,
aiming to maintain visual fidelity. As a result, imperceptible pertur-
bations—which form the basis of many proactive defenses—become
intrinsically expendable under such transformations.

Purification Method

Applying image transformations to an adversarial example ˆ𝑥,
particularly down scaling or compression, inevitably introduces
irreversible modifications to pixel values, including the injected per-
turbations. As demonstrated in Section 3, such transformations can
render the original adversarial perturbations ineffective. In contrast,
natural images typically exhibit redundancy and strong correlations
among neighboring pixels [29, 35], where important features and
structures are often replicated across spatial regions, making critical
information less susceptible to severe degradation. Although naive
downsampling alone is sufficient to invalidate most defense mecha-
nisms, it is generally insufficient to completely remove the residual
perturbations embedded in the image. Consequently, these residual
artifacts may still degrade the output quality of the manipulation
model M, as further illustrated in Fig. 2 and Fig. 3.

approach is to apply existing general super-resolution (SR) models
to adversarial examples ˆ𝑥. However, most existing SR models are

4.2
Transformation-Induced Purification via
Region-wise Super-Resolution
Training or fine-tuning a SR model specifically tailored to protective
perturbations is a feasible alternative. Nevertheless, constructing
paired datasets of clean images and adversarial examples incurs
substantial computational overhead. Moreover, protective pertur-
bations introduced by different protection methods follow distinct
distributions due to their heterogeneous optimization objectives
and strategies. Consequently, the training cost required for such cus-
tomized SR models is typically prohibitive in practical purification
scenarios. Diffusion-based purification methods provide another
line of solutions by injecting a small amount of noise during the
forward diffusion process and recovering clean images through an
iterative reverse denoising procedure [23, 24]. Although these ap-
proaches avoid making explicit assumptions about the perturbation

operations. To avoid directly relying on general SR models while
still leveraging strong structural priors inherent in human faces,

4.3
Experimental Results
4.3.1
Settings and Baselines. The experiments were conducted on
a server running Ubuntu 22.04.4 LTS, equipped with two Intel(R)
Xeon(R) Gold 6133 CPUs clocked at 2.50 GHz and one NVIDIA
GeForce RTX 4090 GPU with 24 GB of memory. We select existing
open-source purification methods, including DiffPure [23], Grid-
Pure [44], and FreqPure [24], as diffusion-based baselines. Com-
parisons with recent super-resolution models are provided in the
appendix. We perform qualitative analysis using the evaluation
metrics introduced in Section 3.
4.3.2
Performance Analysis of TIP-RSR. Experimental results demon-
strate that TIP-RSR consistently outperforms existing purification
methods across a wide range of evaluation metrics. As shown in Ta-
bles 3 and 4, TIP-RSR achieves the best performance among nearly
all defense settings in terms of SSIM, PSNR, FID, and LPIPS. These
results indicate that TIP-RSR is able to effectively suppress adver-
sarial perturbations while largely preserving structural fidelity and
perceptual quality of the input images. It is worth noting that TIP-
RSR performs slightly worse than DiffPure on the BRISQUE metric.
This behavior can be attributed to the fusion of super-resolved
images with adversarial samples at a fixed ratio, which introduces
a mild distribution shift from natural images. Nevertheless, qualita-
tive results confirms that this design leads to improved perceptual
quality, as illustrated in Fig. 6. In contrast, images purified by Diff-
Pure tend to appear overly smooth, resulting in noticeable loss of
fine-grained details.
The primary goal of image purification is to remove defense-
oriented noise such that downstream generative models can pro-
duce higher-quality outputs. The experimental results indicate that
TIP-RSR substantially enhances generation performance. For image
editing tasks, TIP-RSR attains the highest SSIM and PSNR scores
across nearly all settings, suggesting that the purified images pro-
vide more accurate structural guidance, as shown in Table 5. In
addition, TIP-RSR ranks first in terms of FID and LPIPS, indicat-
ing that the purified images serve as high-quality references for
subsequent generative editing. Although TIP-RSR does not always
achieve the absolute best BRISQUE score, its performance remains
consistently close to the optimum, with the worst-case results com-
parable to other purification methods. For TFG task, the purified
images produced by TIP-RSR not only enable high-quality visual
synthesis but also support accurate lip synchronization. As reported
in Table 6, TIP-RSR again achieves the best SSIM and PSNR scores
and shows a clear advantage in terms of FID, ensuring high visual
fidelity of the generated video frames. While its performance on
the Sync-C metric is comparable to other methods, TIP-RSR attains
near-optimal results on M-LMD, leading to more accurate lip motion
and smoother temporal coherence. Moreover, the results highlight

4.3.3
Ablation Study. Ablation Study. We conduct an ablation
study to validate the effectiveness of our proposed TIP-RSR pipeline.
Specifically, we compare it against three core baseline components:
(1) ESRGAN applied directly to the adversarial image (containing
intact perturbations); (2) GFPGAN applied to the JPEG-compressed
and resized version of the adversarial image (where perturbations
have been largely removed); (3)ESRGAN+GFPGAN, a mask-based
fusion of the two outputs.
As shown in Table 7, our full TIP-RSR method consistently
achieves the best or second-best performance across all key met-
rics—including SSIM, PSNR, FID, and LPIPS—on both the Facelock
and Silencer-I adversarial defenses. This demonstrates that TIP-RSR
effectively integrates and surpasses the individual contributions of
its constituent modules.
Critically, TIP-RSR outperforms the ESRGAN+GFPGAN baseline
in most key metrics, despite both approaches combining outputs
from the two branches. This improvement can be attributed to
our method’s adaptive integration strategy, which retains a con-
trolled proportion of information from the original adversarial im-
age through structured feature fusion, rather than relying on a fixed
mask-based blend. By preserving certain high-frequency structural
cues that are otherwise lost in the fully preprocessed GFPGAN
branch, TIP-RSR achieves a better balance between perturbation
suppression and detail fidelity, leading to higher perceptual and
quantitative quality. The results validate that a purposefully de-
signed, adaptive fusion mechanism is more effective than a straight-
forward mask-based combination.
5
Conclusion
In this work, we present a comprehensive analysis of perturbation-
based proactive defense methods for portrait images, using image


Do Protective Perturbations Really Protect Portrait Privacy under Real-world Image Transformations?
Conference’17, July 2017, Washington, DC, USA
editing and talking-face generation (TFG) as representative applica-
tion scenarios. Extensive experimental results indicate that existing
approaches struggle to maintain their effectiveness when subjected
to common real-world transformations, such as scale variations
and color compression. Motivated by these findings, and to further
raise awareness of potential risks, we introduce TIP-RSR, a training-
free purification approach built upon super-resolution techniques.
The proposed method consistently outperforms state-of-the-art
diffusion-based purification baselines while requiring less than one-
tenth of the computational cost. We also encourage the community
to place greater emphasis on evaluating and improving defense
robustness under realistic deployment conditions, particularly in
the presence of diverse and unavoidable image transformations.

A
Protective Perturbations Degrade under
Real-world Image Transformations
To further analyze the robustness of proactive defenses under prac-
tical deployment conditions, we separately evaluate two common
post-defense image transformations: JPEG compression and im-
age resizing. In this setting, Protected denotes directly using the
protected image as input for generation, while Protected + JPEG
and Protected + Resize denote applying JPEG compression or resiz-
ing to the protected image before feeding it into the downstream
generator.
As shown in Tables 8 and 9, once protected images are subjected
to these common real-world transformations, the quality of the gen-
erated outputs consistently improves across both image editing and
talking face generation (TFG) tasks. In most cases, SSIM and PSNR
increase, while FID, LPIPS, and M-LMD decrease, indicating that
the generated results become closer to those obtained from clean
inputs and exhibit better visual fidelity and structural consistency.
These results further support our main conclusion that exist-
ing perturbation-based proactive defenses are highly sensitive to
post-processing operations commonly encountered in real-world
image dissemination. In particular, transformations such as JPEG
compression and resizing tend to partially suppress or remove pro-
tective perturbations while largely preserving the semantic content
of the image, thereby weakening the intended defensive effect.

Analysis of Super-Resolution Model Selection
To justify the model design in TIP-RSR, we compare several rep-
resentative super-resolution (SR) models for adversarial image pu-
rification under the Silencer-I defense setting. The purpose of this
experiment is not simply to identify the newest or strongest SR
model on generic restoration benchmarks, but to determine which
models are most suitable for our purification objective. Different
from standard SR, our task requires not only recovering visual
details, but also suppressing protective perturbations while preserv-
ing identity-related facial structures and maintaining downstream
generative usability.
As shown in Table 11, newer SR models do not necessarily yield
better purification performance in this setting. Although TVT, a re-
cently proposed SR model, achieves competitive restoration quality,

it requires over 27 seconds per image, making it substantially less
practical for our scenario. In contrast, ESRGAN and GFPGAN pro-
vide a more favorable balance between purification effectiveness,
reconstruction quality, and computational efficiency. Specifically,
ESRGAN achieves the highest SSIM and PSNR, indicating stronger
structural fidelity, while GFPGAN obtains the lowest FID and LPIPS,
suggesting better perceptual restoration quality.
These observations are consistent with the design motivation of
TIP-RSR. ESRGAN is more suitable for preserving global structure
and non-facial details, whereas GFPGAN, benefiting from a face-
specific prior, is more effective at restoring realistic facial regions
after perturbation suppression. As further illustrated in Fig. 5, both
models exhibit more favorable restoration behavior than newer al-
ternatives in the adversarial purification setting. Therefore, instead
of adopting the most recent SR model by default, we deliberately
choose ESRGAN and GFPGAN because they better satisfy the prac-
tical requirements of our method: efficiently weakening defensive
perturbations while preserving visually and semantically usable
content.

Comparison with Vision Foundation Models
(VFMs) for Image Purification
To further investigate the practical security implications of our
method, we compare TIP-RSR—a lightweight, training-free purifi-
cation pipeline—with several large-scale vision foundation models
(VFMs) accessed via their official APIs. Unlike TIP-RSR, these VFMs
rely on massive model capacity and extensive training, making
them significantly more computationally expensive and less acces-
sible in real-world scenarios.
As shown in Table 12, despite its simplicity and training-free,
TIP-RSR achieves superior or comparable performance to these
large-scale models. In particular, TIP-RSR attains the highest SSIM
and PSNR, indicating better structural fidelity, while achieving
competitive results on perceptual metrics such as FID and LPIPS. In
contrast, although VFMs exhibit strong generative capabilities, they
fail to consistently recover clean image structures after defensive
perturbations, leading to inferior overall reconstruction quality.
More importantly, this comparison reveals a critical security
concern. TIP-RSR requires no training, minimal computational re-
sources, and can be easily deployed, yet it is sufficient to effectively
suppress protective perturbations and restore high-quality inputs
for downstream generation models. This suggests that existing
perturbation-based defenses can be bypassed by extremely low-cost
purification pipelines, even without access to large-scale models.
Qualitative results in Fig. 8 further support this observation.
Compared to VFM-based purification, TIP-RSR produces cleaner
structures and more natural facial details, indicating that the defen-
sive perturbations are effectively removed.
Overall, these findings highlight a fundamental vulnerability of
current proactive defense methods: their robustness can be com-
promised by simple, efficient, and widely accessible purification
techniques, raising significant concerns about their reliability in
real-world deployment.

Do Protective Perturbations Really Protect Portrait Privacy under Real-world Image Transformations?
Conference’17, July 2017, Washington, DC, USA
Figure 8: Qualitative comparison of purification results between TIP-RSR and vision foundation models (VFMs). TIP-RSR
produces cleaner structures and more natural facial details, indicating more effective removal of protective perturbations.
Abstract: Proactive defense methods protect portrait images from unautho- rized editing or talking face generation (TFG) by introducing pixel- level protective perturbations, and have already attracted increasing attention for privacy protection. In real-world scenarios, images inevitably undergo various transformations during cross-device display and dissemination—such as scale transformations and color compression—that directly alter pixel values. However, it remains unclear whether such pixel-level modifications affect the effec- tiveness of existing proactive defense methods that rely on pixel- level perturbations. To solve this problem, we conduct a systematic evaluation of representative proactive defenses under image trans- formation. The evaluated methods are selected to span different generation architectures such as diffusion and GAN-based models, as well as defense scopes covering both portrait and natural images, and are assessed using both qualitative and quantitative metrics for subjective and objective comparison. Experimental results indicate that defense methods based on pixel-level perturbations struggle to withstand common image transformations, posing a risk of de- fense failure in real-world applications. To further highlight this risk, we propose a simple yet effective purification framework by leveraging the vulnerabilities induced by real-world image trans- formations. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method can efficiently remove protective perturbations with low computational cost, highlighting previously overlooked risks to the research community.
